## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Return a NULL struct when the Arrow evaluator parses a SQL NULL, matching Spark's `from_json`.
This also preserves valid rows in the same batch when the output schema has required fields.

For the target schema `STRUCT<a: BIGINT>`:

| Expression | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ParseJson(NULL)` | `{a: NULL}` | `NULL` |
| `ParseJson('{}')` | `{a: NULL}` | `{a: NULL}` |
| `ParseJson(NULL) IS NULL` | `false` | `true` |
| `COALESCE(ParseJson(NULL), {a: 42})` | `{a: NULL}` | `{a: 42}` |

SQL `COALESCE` selects the first non-NULL value. The SQL NULL case follows
[Spark's explicit null-input handling](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/v4.0.1/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/json/JsonExpressionEvalUtils.scala#L154-L156).

- Decode SQL NULL and the JSON literal `null` into a nullable root struct. Present objects must
  satisfy the required fields in the schema.
- Checkpoints written with `writeStatsAsStruct=true` store a NULL `stats_parsed` for an Add
  without stats. Data skipping keeps such files.

Related to #3116.

## This PR affects the following public APIs

`ParseJsonExpression` specifies root NULL behavior for custom evaluators. The FFI visitor and
protobuf message point to the same contract.

## How was this change tested?

- Expression tests cover SQL NULL, JSON null, empty and populated objects, and required fields
  on Arrow 59 and 60. The synchronous plan exercises `IS NULL` and `COALESCE`.
- A checkpoint round trip with JSON stats disabled checks the Parquet representation and verifies
  that a predicate prunes the populated file while keeping files with missing or empty stats.
- Ran formatting, the kernel library tests, workspace Clippy, and workspace rustdoc.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

**Under Miri, the five `snapshot_log_segment` test cases now take about 6 seconds instead of about 105, a 17x speedup.**

### Problem

These five cases were the most expensive tests in the Miri job. In the latest `main` CI run ([43820557287](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/actions/runs/43820557287)), four of them were among the six slowest of 754 Miri tests, including the slowest (202 seconds). Together the five took 688 seconds, 8.6% of all Miri test time and more than any other test function. Miri was also the slowest job in that run, with one shard taking 18.3 minutes, so Miri test time set how long CI took.

### Cause

`snapshot_log_segment` passes a snapshot's retained file list (paths, sizes, timestamps, and versions) to a C callback. It reads nothing else. But each test case first used `TestTableBuilder` to write a real four-version table, with commits, Parquet data, a checkpoint, and a CRC, and then loaded a snapshot from it. Miri interprets all of that code, even with in-memory storage, and none of it is the `unsafe` FFI code that Miri is there to check.

### Solution

A new test helper, `snapshot_with_fake_log_segment`, builds the `Snapshot` directly from fake log file metadata, so the test writes and reads no files. The five cases and their assertions stay the same. Each file gets its own size and timestamp, so the test fails if the export copies metadata from the wrong file. A comment on the helper explains why it doesn't use `TestTableBuilder`.

In this stack's CI run ([43937867527](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/actions/runs/43937867527)), the five cases took 35 seconds in total, 0.4% of Miri test time.

## How was this change tested?

All five cases pass natively and under Miri, and CI's native and Miri test jobs pass on this branch. The 17x comparison (105 seconds to 6) ran only these five cases, with four test threads on a local machine, so it doesn't measure CI time.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

### Problem

Each Miri shard restores a dependency cache, then recompiles dependencies anyway. That costs about 1-2 minutes per shard, and a Miri shard is usually the last job to finish in the merge queue.

### Cause

Before saving the cache, rust-cache deletes `build/` and `.fingerprint/` directories that don't match a dependency. The pinned version finds the crate name by cutting at the last `-`, which works for stable Cargo's `<crate>-<hash>` names. Miri uses nightly Cargo, which names them `<crate>/<hash>`, so `proc-macro2` becomes `proc`, matches nothing, and gets deleted. Without those fingerprints, Cargo rebuilds the crate and everything that depends on it.

### Solution

Upgrade rust-cache to v2.9.3 in the Miri job; 2.9.2 fixed this cleanup. The other jobs use stable Cargo and keep their pin. The Miri job also fails if cache setup rewrites `Cargo.lock`, because rust-cache runs `cargo metadata` without `--locked`.

### When the speedup appears

Only Miri runs on `main` save the cache, and rust-cache doesn't re-save an exact key match. So Miri keeps restoring the old, incomplete entry until the key changes, usually with the next nightly. The first successful Miri run on `main` after that saves a complete entry, and each shard should then skip 1-2 minutes of dependency compilation. This may take more than a day. Nobody needs to delete caches by hand. #3882 tracks the first save and restore.

## How was this change tested?

I ran the cleanup code from both rust-cache versions on a fake nightly `target/miri` directory. The old version deleted `build/proc-macro2` and `.fingerprint/proc-macro2`; v2.9.3 kept them. The CI speedup can't be measured until `main` saves a new entry.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Add a `full_precision_timestamps` flag to `UnaryExpressionOp::ToJson`. With the flag set,
timestamps keep all six microsecond digits, making `ToJson` the exact inverse of `ParseJson`;
without it, timestamps are truncated to milliseconds as before. The
[AMT RFC](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/pull/3534) will require being able to
serialize timestamp values with full precision. `UnaryExpressionOp::TO_JSON` is the default
(millisecond) form.

Breaking:
- `UnaryExpressionOp::ToJson` is now a struct variant: `ToJson { full_precision_timestamps }`.
- The FFI `EngineExpressionVisitor::visit_to_json` callback takes a `full_precision_timestamps`
  argument.
- The proto `UnaryExpression` message carries a `to_json_full_precision_timestamps` field.

## How was this change tested?

Unit tests for both settings of the flag: timestamp encoding, `ParseJson` round trips, type
errors, `Display`, serde, and proto conversion.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Adds support for `DeltaError` across FFI so core APIs can return `delta_kernel::Result<T>`. Existing `KernelResult<T>` operations use the same FFI result path and retain their numeric Kernel error codes.

Connectors register an `ErrorAllocators` table containing context and separate Kernel/Delta callbacks. `KernelErrorInfo` supplies the code and message, `DeltaErrorInfo` supplies the condition, optional SQLSTATE, named parameters, and rendered message. The outer error variant selects the callback, including when a Delta error has a Kernel cause.

Builders and engines retain a copy of the registration table. Standalone exports borrow one for the call. Callbacks copy any information they retain and return a connector-owned error pointer, which Kernel returns unchanged through `ExternResult::Err`. The connector frees the object. Success calls no allocator, NULL allocation results remain errors.

This PR provides the FFI support for subsequent core API migrations to `Result`, it does not migrate production error conditions or add native engine-cause transport.

### This PR affects the following public APIs

This is a breaking FFI and Rust API change. Connectors must rebuild bindings and supply both allocation callbacks.

- Engine constructors and standalone exports accept `const ErrorAllocators*` in place of `AllocateErrorFn`. REST auth callbacks receive the allocator table pointer as well.
- `ExternResult<T>::Err` carries `void*` instead of `EngineError*`. The `EngineError` type and its required prefix layout are removed.
- Rust allocation methods accept `Error` or `KernelError`, `IntoExternResult` supports both result aliases. `ErrorAllocators::allocate_error` selects the registered Kernel or Delta callback from the outer error variant; `ErrorAllocators::allocate_kernel_error` accepts a Kernel error directly.

### Migration guide for connector authors

1. Regenerate C/C++ headers and language bindings, and rebuild the connector against the matching Kernel library. This changes the FFI ABI.
2. Replace the `AllocateErrorFn` callback with two connector-defined callbacks. Both receive the registered context and borrowed diagnostics, and return a connector-owned `void*`:

   ```c
   // Implement these callbacks in the connector.
   void* connector_kernel_error(void* context, const KernelErrorInfo* info);
   void* connector_delta_error(void* context, const DeltaErrorInfo* info);

   const ErrorAllocators error_allocators = {
       .context = connector_context,
       .allocate_kernel_error = connector_kernel_error,
       .allocate_delta_error = connector_delta_error,
   };

   // Before: get_engine_builder(path, allocate_error)
   // After:
   get_engine_builder(path, &error_allocators);
   ```

   The Kernel callback receives `code` and `message`. The Delta callback receives `condition`, optional `sql_state`, named `parameters`, and `message`. Use the Delta condition or SQLSTATE to classify Delta errors. Copy any diagnostics retained after the callback returns; strings are length-delimited UTF-8, not necessarily NUL-terminated. Both callbacks are required, even if they create the same connector error type.
3. Pass `&error_allocators` wherever an API previously accepted `AllocateErrorFn`, including standalone schema/expression visitors and `allocate_kernel_string`. Update REST authentication callbacks to receive `const ErrorAllocators*` and forward it to `allocate_kernel_string`.
4. Update error-result handling for `ExternResult::Err(void*)`. Remove assumptions that the returned object begins with `EngineError` or a Kernel error code. Interpret and free it using the connector's own error type. A callback may return NULL on allocation failure; `Err(NULL)` still indicates failure.
5. Keep the callback code and context alive for every use, and support concurrent invocation when the engine is shared. Builders and engines copy the table, so its storage only needs to live through registration. Standalone calls borrow it for the call. Callbacks must not unwind across FFI.

For complete C callback implementations and cleanup, see [kernel_utils.c](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/blob/893ebfcf/ffi/examples/common/kernel_utils.c) and [kernel_utils.h](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/blob/893ebfcf/ffi/examples/common/kernel_utils.h).

fn transform_user_defined(

) -> Self::Output<UserDefinedType> {

`snapshot_and_hint` still needs boxed errors because kernel unit tests and the library used by `test_utils` are separate compilations: their `KernelError` types are distinct. ## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Expose `commitInfo.operationMetrics` through the kernel commit-info schema and commit-range action projection.

This also changes the commit-info maps to use `STRING => nullable STRING` values for both `operationParameters` and `operationMetrics`. The Delta protocol leaves `commitInfo` open-ended: "Implementations are free to store any valid JSON-formatted data via the `commitInfo` action." Delta schema serialization also models nullability explicitly; the protocol defines `nullable` for fields and shows map values with `valueContainsNull = true`.

The intended map semantics are:

```text
no operationMetrics key                -> absent/null map
"operationMetrics": null               -> null map, if encountered
"operationMetrics": {}                 -> present empty map
"operationMetrics": {"x":"1"}          -> present map with string value
"operationParameters": {"x": null}     -> present map, key x has null value
```

Kernel-generated commits still write `operationParameters` as an empty map. When kernel has no operation metrics to write, `operationMetrics` is omitted from the commit JSON rather than emitted as `null`.

### This PR affects the following public APIs

`CommitRange` action reads can now include a `commitInfo.operationMetrics` field, and the `commitInfo.operationParameters` / `commitInfo.operationMetrics` maps report nullable values. This is a schema-level change for clients that consume projected commit-info actions directly.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

This PR preserves comparisons over partition-column casts in the predicate passed to checkpoint Parquet handlers.

For example:

```text
CAST(partition_col AS DATE) >= <date>
```

is rewritten to reference the typed checkpoint value:

```text
CAST(add.partitionValues_parsed.<physical_column> AS DATE) >= <date>
```

The handler can then use the predicate for row-group skipping when its CAST and NULL semantics match final query evaluation.

Safety boundaries:

- Only partition columns are rewritten. Data-column casts remain unknown because applying an arbitrary cast to min/max statistics can produce unsound bounds.
- Parquet handlers must prune conservatively. They may use casted footer bounds only when the cast preserves those bounds.
- Unsupported CAST terms remain unknown, while independent safe conjuncts can still prune.

This PR does not add CAST support to the in-memory `DataSkippingFilter` or the default Parquet footer evaluator. The in-memory follow-up is tracked in [#3011](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/issues/3011).

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Parquet checkpoint row-group skipping previously ignored partition columns. As a result, a partition-only predicate such as `part = '2026-07-12'` read the entire checkpoint even though `add.partitionValues_parsed.<col>` has usable footer statistics.

This change rewrites eligible physical partition references to the exact `partitionValues_parsed.<col>` leaf, allowing V1 checkpoints and V2 sidecars to skip row groups that cannot contain matching Adds.

- A partition value serves as both its minimum and maximum. Comparisons and `IS [NOT] NULL` therefore operate directly on the parsed partition leaf.
- Partition comparisons do not need the `IS NULL` guard used for data statistics. Scan checkpoint reads combine the predicate with `add.path IS NOT NULL`, so pruning a non-Add row is safe; commit Removes are read separately and still suppress older Adds.
- Data statistics remain null-guarded because a missing `stats_parsed` value may belong to a live Add whose statistics are unavailable.
- A physically absent partition leaf remains unknown and keeps the row group. A present all-null leaf can be pruned by comparisons and `IS NOT NULL`, while `IS NULL` keeps it.
- FLOAT and DOUBLE partition comparisons remain disabled because Parquet footer bounds omit NaNs. Partition null checks are still eligible.

`build_actions_meta_predicate` also no longer requires a data-statistics schema, allowing partition-only predicates to reach checkpoint pruning. The JSON and Parquet handler contracts clarify that pruning is valid only when conservative evaluation of the complete predicate proves there is no match; unsupported and physically absent references remain unknown.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Adds `ScanBuilder::without_row_transforms()` for connectors that reconstruct logical rows themselves (a configured scan node rather than an expression evaluator) and so never consume `ScanMetadata::scan_file_transforms`.

When set, log replay skips building the per-file transform expressions and the per-row partition-value parse done only to feed them, leaving every `scan_file_transforms` entry `None`. The `transform_spec` is retained so the scan still knows its structure. `Scan::execute()` errors under the opt-out; use `scan_metadata()` for listing. Deletion vectors are unaffected, delivered per file in the scan metadata regardless. The flag lives on `StateInfo` and is serialized so the distributed log-replay path honors it.

Skipping the transform loses no information, because a connector can already assemble everything it does from the public scan APIs:

- the logical output schema (`Scan::logical_schema()`) gives the target columns and their order;
- the physical read schema (`Scan::physical_schema()`) gives the columns read from the data file, carrying their physical names and Parquet field ids under column mapping;
- the logical columns absent from the physical schema are the injected ones (partition columns);
- each scan-file row from `scan_metadata()` carries that file's partition values (keyed by physical name), base row id, and deletion vector (see `scan_row_schema()`).

From these a connector injects partition constants, computes row ids as `base_row_id + row_index`, applies column-mapping renames, and applies deletion vectors itself, so the kernel's per-file expression is redundant for it. A follow-up stacked PR serves the same structure from the kernel as a descriptor so connectors don't re-derive it.

## Benchmark

`cargo bench --bench metadata_bench -- scan_metadata` on `300k-add-files-100-col-partitioned` (300k Add files, 100 columns, partitioned), default path vs. the opt-out:

| case | `scan_metadata` (median) |
|---|---|
| default (builds per-file transforms) | 753 ms |
| `without_row_transforms()` | 459 ms |

~39% faster (~1.64x): the opt-out skips the per-file `parse_partition_values` + `get_transform_expr` build. The win scales with the transform cost (partitioning / column mapping / row tracking); plain tables have no transform to skip and are unaffected.

## How was this change tested?

`cargo test -p delta_kernel`: the opt-out retains the spec while setting the skip flag (partitioned and column-mapped tables), `scan_metadata` lists files with every per-file transform `None`, `execute()` errors, deletion vectors still surface, row-commit-version columns still error at build, and the skip flag round-trips through the distributed serde state. Benchmark coverage added to `metadata_bench`.

## Motivation

Full state reconstruction (FSR) needs a per-row dedup key so that the latest action for each identity wins. Today the key is built imperatively in kernel (`extract_dv_unique_id` and friends). The plan-based engine moves that work out of kernel: kernel emits a plan whose dedup-key column is an `Expression` evaluated by the engine. That requires the key construction to be expressible in the kernel IR.

Each Delta action kind (add/remove, protocol, metaData, domainMetadata, txn) maps to a uniformly-shaped `ARRAY<STRING?>` whose first element identifies the kind — e.g. `[coalesce(add.path, remove.path), dv_storage, dv_inline_id]`, `["domainMetadata", domain]`, `["appTxn", appId]`. `Array(...)` is the primitive that constructs those per-row keys.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Adds the per-row array constructor.

- `VariadicExpressionOp::Array` variant + `Expression::array(exprs)` constructor. Each input contributes one element per output row; all inputs must share the same element type. Requires at least one element — the element type is inferred from the inputs.
- Arrow evaluator that produces a `ListArray` from the per-row evaluation of each input expression.
- FFI `EngineExpressionVisitor::visit_array` callback. The `visit-expression` C example wires `Coalesce` + `ArrayConstructor` enum members (the prior `visit_coalesce` field was unwired in the C example — drive-by fix) so dispatch is exercised end-to-end in CI.

### Public API changes

A new expression variant `VariadicExpressionOp::Array` and constructor `Expression::array`. Adding a variant to the exhaustive `VariadicExpressionOp` enum is a breaking change on its own (cargo-semver-checks `enum_variant_added`); the new non-null `visit_array` field on the `EngineExpressionVisitor` FFI struct is breaking too. Hence `feat!`.

## How was this change tested?

- `cargo +nightly fmt && cargo clippy --workspace --benches --tests --all-features -- -D warnings && cargo doc --workspace --all-features --no-deps`
- Arrow evaluator:
  - Arity sweep (N=1/2/3, mixed col+literal)
  - Output field nullability propagation (including the realistic "nullable input column → nullable element field" path)
  - Empty-batch (0 rows) boundary
  - Struct-typed elements
  - Non-null struct element with a null inner field (verifies `contains_null=false` operates on struct-level validity, not inner field nulls)
  - Null propagation
  - Complex children (arithmetic + sibling-variadic `COALESCE` as inputs; `COALESCE` of two `ARRAY`-of-structs in the realistic dedup-key shape)
  - Error paths (empty inputs, wrong `result_type`, type mismatch, null in non-nullable)
- FFI: the C `visit-expression` example evaluates kernel-built `Coalesce` and `Array` end-to-end against a golden output

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

This PR adds the reverse incremental CRC replay accumulator (build up incremental state) and visitor (visit batches of data and then invoke the accumulator).

This is the building block that lets us now:
- have a CRC at some version X
- have some commits from X to N
- incrementally read commits in reverse from N to X+1 (inclusive) and then apply that CRC-Delta (diff) against the base CRC

Note: This is NOT yet hooked up into Snapshot loading. This change is fully isolated. Thus, integration tests will be coming in the _next_ PR.

## What changes are proposed in this pull request?

Integration tests pinning column-mapping (CM) metadata preservation end-to-end
through the public create-table -> snapshot-reload path. The underlying
preserve/fill/reject logic is unit-tested in `table_features::column_mapping` and
`schema` (`make_physical`); these tests cover the public wiring and on-disk
persistence:

  - complete CM metadata (id + physicalName) preserved verbatim
  - physicalName filled with col-<uuid> when only id is supplied
  - id allocated when only physicalName is supplied
  - sparse preserved ids (1, 5, 100) seed new allocations above the max (101+)
  - CM metadata preserved under nested struct fields

Also loosens `assert_column_mapping_config` to compare maxColumnId against the
schema's actual largest mapping id rather than the total field count. The old
invariant only held when the kernel assigned every id itself; preserving
connector-supplied ids breaks it.

Refs #2377.
## How was this change tested?

New integration tests in kernel/tests/integration/create_table/column_mapping.rs,
run with `cargo test -p delta_kernel --all-features --test integration`. fmt,
clippy, and the full suite pass.
